title: The Smallest Odd Abundant Number is 945
description: Open question OQ-02 of abundant-number-oq-01. A positive integer n is abundant when the sum of its proper divisors exceeds n (Nat.Abundant n : n < ∑ d ∈ n.properDivisors, d). The smallest abundant number is 12, but 12 is even; every abundant number below 945 is even, and the smallest odd abundant number is 945 = 3³·5·7, whose proper divisors sum to 975 > 945 (equivalently σ(945) = 1920 > 1890 = 2·945). This is OEIS A005231. The entry proves IsLeast {n | Odd n ∧ Nat.Abundant n} 945. The two large finite computations — that 945 is abundant, and that no odd n < 945 is abundant — are discharged with native_decide over a List-based proper-divisor sum (pdSum, structural recursion, no Quotient), because kernel decide over the full 945-range exhausts the reduction stack under the pinned toolchain. native_decide introduces the Lean.ofReduceBool axiom, so this entry is axiomatized, not axiom-free. 7 theorems, 1 definition, 0 literal axiom declarations, 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext: A number is abundant if its proper divisors sum to more than itself — the excess σ(n) − 2n > 0 measures the abundance. The smallest abundant number is 12 (formalised in the parent abundant-number-oq-01), and small abundant numbers are conspicuously even: 12, 18, 20, 24, 30, …. The first odd abundant number is 945 = 3³·5·7, a fact going back to the classical study of abundant numbers (OEIS A005231). Odd abundant numbers are rare and were historically hard to find precisely because the smallest is already fairly large and must avoid the factor 2 that makes even numbers abundant so easily (a single factor of 2 contributes heavily to σ). The claim 'the smallest odd abundant number is 945' is a bounded but genuinely large finite verification: it requires checking abundance at 945 and non-abundance across all 472 odd numbers below it.
overview.problemStatement: **OQ-02 of abundant-number-oq-01 (smallest odd abundant number).** Prove that 945 is the least odd abundant number: IsLeast {n : ℕ | Odd n ∧ Nat.Abundant n} 945. Equivalently, 945 is odd and abundant (its proper divisors sum to 975 > 945), and no odd n < 945 is abundant.
overview.proofStrategy:
**A kernel-friendly divisor sum (pdSum).** Computing ∑ d ∈ n.properDivisors, d directly under decide forces the kernel to reduce Finset.filter / Finset.sum over Finset.range n — a Quotient-backed computation the kernel reduces very slowly, and which exhausts the native reduction stack (build aborts with signal 135) over the full 945-range. Instead pdSum n := ((List.range n).filter (· ∣ n)).sum uses structural List recursion plus GMP-accelerated Nat.mod, with no Quotient.

**The symbolic bridge (listRange_filter_sum_eq, pdSum_eq).** listRange_filter_sum_eq proves ((List.range n).filter (p ·)).sum = ∑ i ∈ (Finset.range n).filter p, i by induction (List.range_succ / List.filter_append on the List side, Finset.range_succ / Finset.filter_insert on the Finset side), so it does not depend on exact Mathlib lemma names. pdSum_eq then identifies pdSum n = ∑ d ∈ n.properDivisors, d for n ≠ 0 via Nat.filter_dvd_eq_properDivisors — once, symbolically, never under decide.

**The finite computations (abundant_945, check_odd_below).** abundant_945 rewrites Nat.Abundant 945 through pdSum_eq and closes 945 < pdSum 945 by native_decide. check_odd_below : ∀ n < 945, Odd n → pdSum n ≤ n is likewise native_decide; the Odd n hypothesis is evaluated first so even cases short-circuit without computing pdSum.

**Assembling minimality (not_abundant_odd_below, smallest_odd_abundant).** not_abundant_odd_below transports check_odd_below back to Nat.Abundant via pdSum_eq. smallest_odd_abundant then pairs membership (odd_945, abundant_945) with the lower bound, discharging the ordering by contradiction against not_abundant_odd_below.

**Verification status.** The two native_decide calls introduce Lean.ofReduceBool: the entry is axiomatized. The bridge lemmas and odd_945 are ordinary kernel proofs.
keyInsights: The mathematical content is entirely a bounded finite check, but a *naive* kernel decide over Nat.Abundant is infeasible: reducing Finset.filter/Finset.sum over Finset.range 945 is Quotient-backed and blows the native reduction stack (signal 135) under the pinned Lean/Mathlib v4.26 toolchain. The engineering contribution is a kernel-friendly reformulation, not a new theorem.

pdSum trades Quotient-backed Finset machinery for a plain List.range structural recursion with GMP-accelerated Nat.mod — a representation the compiler can evaluate quickly. The correctness price is a single symbolic bridge lemma proved once by induction, entirely off the decide path.

The Odd n hypothesis inside check_odd_below is a deliberate short-circuit: placed before the pdSum comparison, it discharges the ~472 even cases immediately, so the expensive proper-divisor sum is only computed on the odd candidates that actually matter.

Honesty about native_decide: the two large computations are delegated to the compiler, so the proof depends on Lean.ofReduceBool and the entry is axiomatized (badge: axiom), even though there are 0 literal axiom declarations (leanFile.axiomCount = 0) and 0 sorries. This is the conservative reading of the project's native_decide policy.

The split between kernel-checked scaffolding (the bridge lemmas, odd_945, the minimality assembly) and compiler-checked leaves (abundant_945, check_odd_below) localises the Lean.ofReduceBool dependency to exactly the two unavoidable finite enumerations.

sections.title: A kernel-friendly proper-divisor sum
sections.summary: pdSum n := ((List.range n).filter (fun d => decide (d ∣ n))).sum — the List-based sum of the proper divisors of n, defined over List.range so the compiler can evaluate it without Finset/Quotient overhead. This is the object the two native_decide computations actually run on.
sections.mathContext: $\mathtt{pdSum}\,n = \sum_{d < n,\ d \mid n} d$, computed by structural recursion on a List with GMP-accelerated divisibility tests — no Quotient.

sections.title: The symbolic bridge to properDivisors

conclusion.summary: Proves that 945 = 3³·5·7 is the smallest odd abundant number: IsLeast {n | Odd n ∧ Nat.Abundant n} 945. The two large finite computations (945 is abundant; no odd n < 945 is) are discharged with native_decide over a kernel-friendly List-based proper-divisor sum pdSum, bridged symbolically to Mathlib's Nat.Abundant. Because native_decide introduces Lean.ofReduceBool, the entry is axiomatized (badge: axiom, meta.axiomCount = 1); it has 0 literal axiom declarations (leanFile.axiomCount = 0) and 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: A worked template for large bounded number-theoretic verifications that are infeasible under kernel decide: reformulate the Quotient-backed Finset computation as a structural List recursion, prove a one-off symbolic bridge lemma off the decide path, and delegate the enumeration to native_decide — accepting the Lean.ofReduceBool dependency and marking the entry axiomatized honestly. The pdSum / listRange_filter_sum_eq pair is reusable for any divisor-sum or filtered-count verification over a large range.
openQuestions: A kernel-only (Lean.ofReduceBool-free) verification of the same result — e.g. via a smarter decidable procedure or a Fin-indexed reflection — that would upgrade the entry from axiomatized to verified.
The smallest odd abundant number not divisible by 3 (7241·... — 5391411025), a dramatically larger bounded search that would stress the pdSum approach far beyond 945.
The density of odd abundant numbers and the least odd weird number, both natural follow-ons to the least odd abundant number established here.
